source.title: Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable, Empirically
source.authors: Joel Hestness; Sharan Narang; Newsha Ardalani; Gregory Diamos; Heewoo Jun; Hassan Kianinejad; Md. Mostofa Ali Patwary; Yang Yang; Yanqi Zhou

record.tranche_reason: The study measures validation error as training-set size grows and fits learning curves, but it does not reproduce parameter-count or compute scaling laws.
record.gate_note: Rows record the study's own validation-error scaling results. Cited results from other work are excluded. Model-size growth with training-set size is not included because it does not measure a listed claim version.
record.test_reason: Pre-dates both originals. It measures held-out word and character LM cross-entropy as training-set size grows over about 2.6 orders of magnitude. Model size is re-tuned per shard, so parameters are not the bottleneck. This bears on V1's token axis. It repeats the measurement for translation, ImageNet and speech (V5) and reports bends away from the trend that depend on tuning and on metric (V7). It does not vary parameters or compute as the scaled variable and has no held-out extrapolation test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that generalization error falls as a power law in training-set size across all four domains, architectures, optimizers and loss functions. Exponents (−0.07 to −0.35) are domain-specific and unexplained by theory. Within a domain, architecture and optimizer changes shift the curve but not the exponent. Best-fit model size grows sublinearly with data. Curves have a small-data region at best-guess level and an irreducible-error floor, which was not reached in this study. Large-data departures are attributed to optimization difficulty, fixable by more tuning.
record.recipe_differences: Measures validation error as training-set size changes and searches for best-fit model sizes; it does not test held-out pretraining cross-entropy against parameter count or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported exponents differ by domain and metric; character-LM optimizer choice slightly changes the exponent and shifts the curve; large-set optimization difficulty causes departures from fitted trends.

fits_no_version.finding: Within a domain, different architectures share the same data-scaling exponent: 2- vs 4-layer LSTM and RHN word LMs, and DS2 vs attention speech models. The 4-layer LSTM is about 1.5% worse in level.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture changes shift the intercept of data-scaling learning curves but not their exponent.

fits_no_version.finding: Best-fit model size grows sublinearly with data size: βp ≈ 0.69 for word LMs (0.78 for the 4-layer LSTM), 0.78/0.92 for character LMs, and 0.573 for ResNets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameter count needed to fit a dataset grows as a sublinear power of data size.

record.problems: The authors report that larger models and data sets become harder to optimize, curves depart from power-law trends at the largest language-model shards, and exhaustive hyperparameter search would be needed to bring results closer to the trend. The study does not test parameter-count or compute scaling laws, nor out-of-range extrapolation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out.

untested.parts: Loss scaling with parameter count or compute as the scaled variable; single-epoch large-scale pretraining.
Entire version: no held-out test of small-run fits predicting much larger runs.
Entire version: no fixed-compute allocation. The sublinear best-fit model size vs data result is not a compute-optimal frontier.
No comparison of shapes at fixed parameter count.
Video, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes.
Parameter-counting conventions, training schedule, fitting-method comparisons, and disagreement between published laws.

missing.what: Single-model-size NMT learning curves fit power law plus constant: 17M params βg −0.36, 48M params βg −0.30. The composite best-fit curve gives −0.128. Exponent depends on whether model size is held fixed or re-tuned.

Fixed-size DS2 curves plateau as data grows: 1.7M params at about 170 h, 6M params at about 860 h. The 87M model stays near the best-fit trend. This shows the bottleneck effect when model size is fixed.
NMT without dropout gives 'similar learning curve exponents' (regularizer insensitivity).
Table 1 exponents differ from the text: word LM RHN −0.070, attention speech −0.296.

record.verdict_notes: Data-scaling only, trained to convergence with multi-epoch passes on small shards, unlike the single-epoch setup of Kaplan et al. The V1 verdict covers the token axis only. The tranche could arguably be T3, since the study pre-dates the originals. Its claim that 'model improvements only shift the error' rests on few architecture pairs.

versions.untested_parts: Tests data-size scaling for language models, but not loss scaling with parameter count or training compute, and does not independently establish that the other factors are not bottlenecks.
No held-out extrapolation test in which fits from small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
Does not compare parameter/token allocations at fixed compute or estimate their growth with compute.
Compares architectures, but does not compare them at a fixed parameter count as this version specifies.
Tests learning curves in machine translation, image classification, and speech recognition, but not video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream-task performance relationship is tested.
Reports exponent variation across domains, metrics, and some model/optimizer settings, and reports curve divergence; does not systematically compare parameter-counting or fitting methods.

rows.subject: Word language models
rows.operation_detail: Measured validation cross-entropy as training-set size increased.

conditions.value: 10% of the Billion Word Dataset

rows.measure: Departure of validation loss from the fitted power-law trend
rows.value: Models began to diverge from power-law scaling at 10% of the Billion Word benchmark; larger-set results settled at or just above the trend after additional tuning.
rows.note: The authors attribute the deviation to increasing optimization difficulty and say more hyperparameter search may bring models closer to the trend.
rows.check: Departure at about 10% of Billion Word is largely closed by extra batch-size and learning-rate tuning ('settle at or just above the trend'). For V7 this is a bend that depends on a training choice, so it is partial.

source_check.correct: V1: partial before additional tuning. V7: observed. Word LMs depart at the 10% shard; additional batch-size and learning-rate tuning brings tuned word models to or just above the trend.
source_check.problem: Partial fits V1; the tuning-dependent departure is an observed instance of V7.

rows.subject: Neural machine translation sequence-to-sequence model with global attention
rows.operation_detail: Trained on increasing shards of WMT’16 German-to-English data and measured validation error.

conditions.value: 4.5 million training sequences; roughly 130 million tokens in each language before shard selection

rows.measure: Per-token classification error; composite best-fit learning-curve exponent
rows.note: The composite curve uses the best-fit model at each training-set size.
rows.check: The −0.128 is a projected composite fit ('if we project forward'), measured on token error rather than loss. Single-model curves fit power-law plus constant with −0.36 and −0.30, which is not recorded. The V7 link is dropped from this row; the single-model vs composite contrast goes under missing.

source_check.problem: The approximate −0.128 exponent is explicitly a forward projection of the composite curve, not a separately validated extrapolation.
